artboards.title: As it stands today — a ledger with a form on top
Proposed — the position, the shape of the period, and the ranking
Proposed — by customer, and by document
Proposed — nothing sold, nothing judgeable, and a failed read

annotations.text:
THE JOB OF THIS SCREEN

You told me four things in the interview, and everything on the artboard to the right follows from them.

1. YOU OPEN IT ASKING "WHO AND WHAT MAKES ME MONEY." So it is a RANKING, ordered on gross profit -- what you kept, not what you turned over. Today it lands on a date-ordered list of invoices, which answers a different question entirely.

2. IT IS EVIDENCE, NOT A VERDICT. Analysis judges and tells you what to fix. This screen does not grow opinions: no findings queue, no badges, no advice. It orders the facts honestly and gets out of the way. The one thing it does do is declare its order, in the panel header, so you can argue with it.

3. ONE CHART, AND IT DRAWS THE PERIOD'S SHAPE. Thirty bars, one a day, with the previous window's daily average as a dashed line. It is the only thing on the screen a table genuinely cannot show -- and it is the thing that turns "sales are down 8%" into "the whole fall is in the last nine days."

4. IT IS A DESK SCREEN. The phone is a competent reading fallback, drawn from scratch at 390, not a reflow.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Analysis, Debtors, Pricing, Consignment and Creditors. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no fourteenth button family.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS >
The eight markers on the artboard.

1. A 140-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH, UNMEASURED, OPEN ON EVERY VISIT. Seven screens already put the long version behind the "i" bubble and keep a one-line sub. This is one of the ones left.

2. THE SCREEN'S ONE ACCENT IS SPENT ON A FORM SUBMIT. The oxide is meant to appear once, on the thing to do next. Here it is on "Search" -- and that button is half a lie: every preset re-renders on change, so it does nothing at all unless you picked Custom. The one real action on the screen, Export CSV, is a ghost button in the corner.

3. FIVE TILES AND NO SHAPE. "Cost of item sold" is Items sales minus Gross profit, printed because it can be. Meanwhile nothing on the screen says whether the month was steady, front-loaded, or dying -- and 148,600,000 on its own is either a good month or a collapse.

4. THREE SUB-TABS OF THE SAME NINE-COLUMN TABLE. Doc, item, customer: same columns, same weight, no answer. It is a spreadsheet with a sort header, and the sorting is left to you.

5. IT LANDS ORDERED BY DATE. The default view is "Statistics by doc." sorted newest-first -- a ledger. Nothing on the screen answers "who and what makes me money" until you switch tab and click a column yourself.

6. A SALE THAT LOST MONEY SITS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE LIST WEARING NOTHING. INV-0407 is 124,000 down. It is the single most interesting row on the screen and it is the sixth one, because the sort is on date.

7. NO TOTALS UNTIL YOU HAVE SCROLLED 214 ROWS. The total row is real and correct -- and it is at the bottom of every row in the range, so the only practical way to see what a column adds up to is to export it and open a spreadsheet.

8. NO CHART, ANYWHERE. A screen called analytics that never draws time.

WHAT IS ALREADY RIGHT, AND IS KEPT: the estimated-cost honesty. anCostConfidence, the * on the row, and the sentence that says most of a margin can rest on a guess -- that is the best thing on this screen and the redesign promotes it rather than moving it.

THE PROPOSAL -- what changed, and why

IT LANDS AS A RANKING, ON GROSS PROFIT. By item, ordered on what you kept, and the panel header says so in words: "ranked by gross profit." An order you cannot see is an order you cannot disagree with. Cement is first on 5,520,000 kept; iron sheets, the biggest thing you sell at 31,961,600 of turnover, is third -- because it only keeps 9.3%. That inversion is the whole reason you chose profit over sales, and it is visible in the first three rows.

THE ROW IS CUT TO WHAT EARNS ITS PLACE. Name, what it sold, what it made, what it kept, the margin. Cost of item sold comes off the screen -- it is one subtraction away and it was costing a column of a 13px table. Variant, category and unit fold into the item's own meta line, where they identify the thing rather than competing with the money. Export CSV still writes all nine columns and all 147 rows, so nothing is lost where it is actually used.

THE MONEY COLUMNS NEVER TRUNCATE; THE NAME GIVES WAY. Tabular mono, right-aligned, sized to content, with min-width:0 on the name so it ellipsises instead of pushing the figures out of the box. "1,240,00" is a tenth of "1,240,000" and looks entirely plausible.

THE TOTAL ROW IS PINNED. It sits under the scroll region, not at the bottom of 147 rows. You can see what the column adds up to without leaving the screen, and it carries the same * as the rows it adds up.

THE STRIP IS THE POSITION, AND THE FIFTH TILE IS THE TRUST. Cost of item sold gives up its tile to the figure that says how much of all this rests on a guess: 1,206 of 8,940 units, 13% of what you sold. That was a footnote under the figures it undermines; it is now beside them. Past half, the tile goes amber -- see state B.

THE DELTAS ARE INK, NOT COLOUR. Today "-8%" prints crimson and "+3%" verdigris. But turnover down 8% while profit is up 3% is not bad news -- it is the best sentence on the screen. Colouring the arrow crimson would have told you the opposite of what happened. Crimson is kept for the genuinely bad: the one loss-making figure, in the document view.

THE CHART DRAWS THE SUBTRACTION, AND SAYS IT FIRST. The sentence comes before the bars -- 3,100,000 a day since 27 August against 5,750,000 before it -- and the bars prove it. One series, one grey; the near-empty bars are Sundays and are drawn in the hairline grey so a closed day does not read as a collapse. The dashed line is the previous window's daily average. Nothing is recoloured, because position already carries the meaning.

AND THE FOOTNOTE UNDER THE CHART IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: this counts on the day the invoice was raised, not the day it was paid. A strong week sold on credit shows here in full, and the money for it may not exist. The current screen never says this anywhere.

THE ACCENT APPEARS ONCE, ON EXPORT CSV. On an evidence screen, taking the evidence away IS the thing to do next. "Search" stops being a button and the range becomes a plain control, which is what it always was.

HEIGHT: the current screen needs the whole page scrolled to reach the total. The position, the shape of the period, ten ranked rows and the pinned total now fit above 1,105px.

ARITHMETIC, so it survives being checked: 1,840 bags at 20,000 is 36,800,000, at a 17,000 cost keeps 5,520,000 -- 15.0%. 704 sheets at 45,400 against 41,200 keeps 2,956,800 -- 9.3%, the same figures Analysis already carries. The ten rows shown total 132,109,600 of the window's 148,600,000, so they fit inside it. The thirty daily bars sum to 148,600,000 exactly, and the last nine to 27,900,000, which is the 3,100,000 a day the sentence claims.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. IT LANDS ON "BY ITEM". Item and customer both answer "who and what makes me money"; the screen has to open on one. I chose item because an item's margin is in your own hands -- you set the price, you choose the supplier -- where a customer ranking mostly tells you who to keep. One line of code if you would rather land on customer.

2. COST OF ITEM SOLD IS OFF THE SCREEN. It is in the export, and it is Items sales minus Gross profit. If you read it across the row often enough that the subtraction is a nuisance, say so and it comes back -- it costs the "Sold" column.

3. THE FIFTH TILE'S AMBER THRESHOLD IS HALF. Under half the units estimated, the tile is ink; over half, amber, and the profit and margin stop being printed at all (state B). Half is a guess at where a margin stops being worth stating. You know better than I do.

4. THE CHART IS DAILY. Thirty bars at 30 days; at 90 or "all time" it has to become weekly or monthly, and I have not drawn the switch. The honest options are: bucket automatically by span, or say "weekly" in the panel note and let it change under you.

5. THE SCROLL REGION IS TEN ROWS. Enough that the total stays on screen with the chart above it. If you would rather see fifteen and lose the chart's sentence, that is a real trade.

6. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: anInvoicesInRange, invoiceLineCost and the FIFTH-lot costing, anCostConfidence, anPreviousTotals, anFilterRows, the CSV, or the voided-invoice exclusion. This is a design, not a rewrite -- the same readings feed it, and every figure on the artboard is one the existing code already computes.

7. A BUG I FOUND ON THE WAY. .ow-mini in index.html (around line 7960) carries both border-top and max-width:76ch, so on any panel wider than the measure its hairline stops in mid-air. It is visible on this screen's 1,116px panels. The rule belongs to the panel and the measure to the text; drawn correctly here.

THE OTHER TWO VIEWS >

You kept all three tabs, so both of the others are drawn rather than asserted.

BY CUSTOMER IS THE SAME MACHINE. Ranked on gross profit, location in the meta line, invoice count where "Sold" was. And it makes the case for the ranking better than the item view does: Kato is the biggest name on the list, 28,640,000 of turnover, and holds one of its thinnest margins. On the old screen, sorted by sales, Kato is first and looks like your best customer.

BY DOCUMENT KEEPS ITS DATE ORDER, DELIBERATELY. You said you use it to check a single sale's profit without opening it. That is a lookup, not a question, so it stays newest-first and the header says what it is: "a ledger, not a ranking." The per-view sort state the code already keeps makes this free.

AND IT IS THE ONLY VIEW THAT SHOWS YOU A SALE THAT LOST MONEY. INV-0407, 124,000 down, 7.9% under. No ranking by item or by customer would ever surface it -- it is buried inside Kato's 5,441,600 and inside cement's 5,520,000. That is the argument for keeping this tab, and it is worth more than the argument you gave me.

THE COLUMN SETS DIFFER ONLY IN THE IDENTITY COLUMNS. Item: name / sold. Customer: name / invoices. Document: date / doc no. / customer. The four money columns are identical across all three, in the same order, right-aligned in the same widths -- so switching tabs never moves a figure you were reading.

THE THREE STATES A SCREEN IS ONLY DESIGNED ONCE YOU HAVE DRAWN >

A. NOTHING SOLD, AND NO STRIP OF ZEROS. Five tiles reading 0 says the shop is broken. It is not -- so the screen says what it knows instead: 19 invoices in the seven days before this window, worth 22,940,000, and the two reasons the range might be empty. One of them is the one that actually catches people: an order that was never turned into an invoice does not exist to this screen, and nothing currently says so.

B. THE BOOKS CANNOT JUDGE IT. This is the honesty device taken to its conclusion. When two thirds of the units sold have no purchase cost on file, the margin is not merely uncertain -- it is fiction, and the current screen would print it to one decimal place: 62%. So gross profit and gross margin read "not stated", in the tile, in the total row and in the export, while turnover and the count -- which are real -- are shown as normal. Three amber tiles, which is loud, but they are one condition, not three.

C. THE BOOKS FAILED TO READ. This state does not exist today: if the sales ledger fails, the screen draws the same empty panels a quiet month draws, and those are not the same news. The app's own law is that a failure must name itself. So it says what failed, when the last good read was, and that nothing is shown from it -- a figure with no date on it is worse than no figure.

EACH OF THESE IS A WHOLE SCREEN, so each carries its own single accent. That is two oxide buttons on this artboard, one each on the two states that have something to do. B has none: there is no button that puts a buy price on 1,604 lines.

THE PHONE -- a reading fallback, and honest about it >

You said this is a desk screen. So the 390 design is not a second full app competing with the desktop; it is the two things a phone is for here -- where you stand, and what the list says -- drawn from scratch at 390 rather than reflowed.

820px is a switch: 44px navy bar, 26px Archivo page name, 15px row titles, 14-16px padding, cards instead of 34px rows, a white 60px tab bar whose active mark is FILLED rather than merely coloured. No fake status bar and no fake keyboard -- the real ones render on top of this.

WHAT IS DROPPED, DELIBERATELY: the chart, the customer and document views, the export, and five of the six columns. Thirty bars at 390px is a smudge, and reading a nine-column table one-handed in a yard is not a thing anyone does.

WHAT SURVIVES: the 2x2 position in one card with hairline dividers and no per-tile border, the chart's SENTENCE without the chart, three ranked items, and the account of what is missing -- "144 more items, 19,492,000 kept between them." A phone shows fewer rows than a desk; it must say so, and say what it is holding back.

THERE IS NO ACCENT ON THIS SCREEN, and that is not an oversight. The accent is the one thing to do next, and on a reading screen with the export dropped there is nothing to do. An oxide button here would have to be pointing at something.
